region: Indonesia — Bali and the Lesser Sunda Islands
description: Named for the island of Solor in Indonesia; terminal males develop a fiery red head over a violet-blue body and flare their fins at females during late-afternoon courtship. Like other fairy wrasses it spends the night wrapped in a mucus cocoon among rubble.

region: Western Pacific — mainly the Philippines
description: A Philippine fairy wrasse of rubble slopes; terminal males are orange-pink with deep red dorsal and pelvic fins that they raise like banners while displaying to their harem.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & eastern Indonesia
description: One of the smaller fairy wrasses, living in loose groups a few metres above rubble on outer reef slopes. Displaying males turn intense magenta with a yellow-orange back and flare their dark pelvic fins.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus, north to southern Japan
description: The most widespread fairy wrasse, and its colours differ noticeably between Indian Ocean and Pacific populations. A dark spot on the upper caudal peduncle marks both sexes, and displaying males light up with electric-blue lines.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan to Indonesia, east to Fiji & Tonga
description: One of the largest fairy wrasses, usually found on rubble slopes below about 20 m. Males are pink to lavender with yellow-centred dorsal, anal and caudal fins boldly edged in red.

region: Western & central Pacific — Great Barrier Reef to the Pitcairn Islands
description: Ranges further east than most fairy wrasses, from the Great Barrier Reef to Pitcairn. Terminal males are vividly red, purple and green and spend much of the day displaying to the females of their harem.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Endemic to Hawaii, where it lives over rubble and sand patches on deeper reef slopes. Terminal males are flame-red above shading to yellow below, while females are paler and pinker.

region: Coral Sea — Great Barrier Reef & New Caledonia
description: A Coral Sea species of deeper rubble slopes, notable for the long, lance-shaped tail of the male. Males are golden-yellow with fine purple-blue lines running along the flank.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Andaman Sea to the Philippines & southern Japan
description: Lives in large mixed aggregations above reef slopes, picking zooplankton from the current. The name means "blue side", for the bright blue-edged scales on the forward flank of displaying males.

region: Coral Sea — New Caledonia & the Great Barrier Reef
description: Named for the French diver and photographer Pierre Laboute, it is known mainly from New Caledonia and the southern Great Barrier Reef. Males are rosy pink with bold magenta and yellow stripes along the flank.

region: Red Sea & western Indian Ocean to Sri Lanka
description: A small fairy wrasse that forms large, busy aggregations just above the reef, hence its common name. Males have greatly elongated red pelvic fins that trail beneath the body during display.

region: Micronesia — Caroline, Mariana & Marshall Islands
description: A Micronesian fairy wrasse whose name means "yellow-striped", for the golden band along the upper flank that stands out against the male's magenta-purple body.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia & Palau
description: A small fairy wrasse of rubble slopes; the male's bright yellow dorsal fin and yellow-washed back contrast sharply with its pink to red body.

region: Indonesia — Java, Bali & Sulawesi
description: Males carry long whip-like filaments on the dorsal fin, which they raise while racing around their females in display. The body shades from red-orange above to violet-blue below.

region: Western Pacific — Papua New Guinea & the Great Barrier Reef to Fiji & Tonga
description: Often found in shallower lagoon and back-reef rubble than its deep-water relatives. Both sexes are peppered with fine dark spots, and males develop violet tones and long pelvic fins.

region: Indonesia — northern Sulawesi & the Molucca Sea
description: Described in 1999 from northern Sulawesi; displaying males have a vivid orange back and dorsal fin over a magenta-purple lower body.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan & Taiwan
description: A rarely exported fairy wrasse from deep reef slopes of southern Japan and Taiwan; males are distinguished by a long, lance-shaped tail and a pink body washed with yellow above.

region: Micronesia — Marshall Islands & Pohnpei
description: Known from deeper outer-reef slopes in the Marshall Islands and Pohnpei. Males are golden yellow with violet-edged fins and a diamond-shaped (rhomboid) tail.

region: Central Indian Ocean — Chagos Archipelago & Maldives
description: Described from the Chagos Archipelago and exported mainly from the Maldives. Its name ("red scales") refers to the patch of crimson scales on the male's lower forward flank.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia, Palau & southern Japan
description: Males hold harems over rubble and, especially in late afternoon, "flash" — racing above the females with every fin spread and colours briefly intensified. The tall red dorsal fin carries a few elongated rays.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands & Great Barrier Reef
description: Named for the many long filaments that trail from the male's dorsal fin and are raised during display flights over the harem. Forms mixed groups with other flashers and fairy wrasses over rubble.

region: Indian Ocean & western Pacific — East Africa to Indonesia
description: Unlike many flashers, the male has no long filaments; instead its tall, sail-like dorsal fin is red with an electric-blue border. Courting males flash over rubble patches in the late afternoon.

region: Red Sea (endemic)
description: A Red Sea endemic named for the eight blue-violet lines along its orange flanks. The male's dorsal fin is tall and rounded rather than filamentous.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: Its blue flank lines are broken into rows of dots and dashes, which separates it from the similar Carpenter's flasher. Males display over rubble in late afternoon with all fins spread.

region: Indonesia — Sulawesi, Halmahera & Raja Ampat
description: Described in 1999 from Indonesia; when flashing, males turn an intense violet-blue below an orange-red back.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines
description: Males are told apart from other flashers by their bright yellow anal fin beneath an orange-red, blue-lined body. Like its relatives it lives in harems a metre or two above rubble.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: Named for the angular outline of the male's dorsal fin. Displaying males show orange-red flanks with blue lines and a deep red dorsal fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Darts constantly among rock crevices hunting tiny crustaceans, pest flatworms and pyramid snails, and sleeps in a mucus cocoon. Often turns into a persistent bully toward smaller, more peaceful fish.

region: Central & western Pacific — Micronesia to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: A secretive cousin of the sixline wrasse with four bright blue stripes on a bronze upper body above a violet belly. Notably aggressive toward other small wrasses.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: The largest Pseudocheilinus, recognised by eight thin dark lines on a pinkish body. An efficient hunter of pest snails and bristleworms that grows more aggressive with age.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: Also called the disappearing wrasse: it lives deep in rubble and coral heads and is rarely seen in the open. Reddish with fine pale striations and a white streak below the eye.

region: Western & central Pacific — Philippines & Micronesia to Samoa
description: A deep-reef wrasse, usually below 20 m, with a violet forebody fading into a yellow rear and a black eyespot near the tail. Comparatively rarely collected and highly prized.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: A tiny, secretive wrasse of sheltered inshore reefs, purple with pinkish streaks along the flank. It stays close to rock and coral cover and is one of the most peaceful wrasses for small reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas & Pitcairn
description: Creeps through caves and crevices rather than swimming in the open, rarely leaving cover. Yellow-ringed black eyespots on the rear dorsal, anal and pelvic fins likely misdirect predators.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: A smaller, deeper-living relative of the sharpnose possum wrasse with narrow white rather than yellow bars. It lives deep within reef crevices and is seldom seen by divers.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Runs cleaning stations visited by hundreds of reef fish a day, advertising with a bobbing dance and removing parasites and dead tissue. Most wild-caught individuals fail to adapt to aquarium diets, so its collection is widely discouraged.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Hawaii's endemic cleaner wrasse, more colourful than its widespread relative with a yellow head and a magenta-violet rear half. It services a wide range of reef fish at fixed cleaning stations.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Line Islands & Marquesas
description: Unlike the bluestreak cleaner it roams widely instead of holding a fixed station, cleaning fish across a large home range. Adults are dark in front and pale yellow behind, with a dark crescent in the tail.

region: Red Sea & Gulf of Aden
description: Juveniles are dedicated cleaners of other fish, but adults switch to feeding mainly on coral polyps. Its deep blue body bears two electric-blue lines along each side.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: A thick-lipped wrasse that feeds on live coral polyps and mucus, while juveniles also clean other fish part-time. Adults have a golden-yellow back and a pale wedge in the tail.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii
description: A slender, fast-swimming wrasse that dives into the sand to sleep. Females are salmon-pink, while terminal males turn blue-green with a yellow-and-blue stripe along the lower flank.

region: Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Maldives & Sri Lanka to Indonesia
description: Named after underwater photographer Mike Severns. A slender sand-sleeping wrasse whose terminal males are greenish blue with fine lines, while females are orange-pink.

region: Pacific — Indonesia to the Line Islands & the eastern Pacific
description: A restless forager of shallow reef flats that is almost never still. Both sexes carry a bright red-orange mark above the pectoral fin — the "red shoulder".

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: Endemic to Hawaii and Johnston Atoll, where it forages over shallow reef flats. Terminal males are green with a bright orange belt along the flank edged by blue lines.

region: Pacific — Cocos-Keeling & Christmas Islands to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: Its long, tubular snout probes coral branches and crevices for small crustaceans and brittle stars. Males are deep blue-green, while females are pale in front shading to black behind with an orange upper snout.

region: Indian Ocean — Red Sea & East Africa to the Andaman Sea
description: The Indian Ocean counterpart of the Pacific bird wrasse, using its long beak to pick prey from coral crevices. Males are deep blue; females are paler with a dark rear and finely spotted flanks.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Christmas Island to the Marshall Islands, Japan to Australia
description: A bright yellow wrasse that dives into the sand at night or when frightened, and may stay buried for days after being moved. Prized in reef tanks for picking off flatworms and other small pests.

region: Indian Ocean — Maldives & Sri Lanka to western Indonesia
description: Named for its two-tone colouring — lemon-yellow above, white below — with black spots on the dorsal fin. Like other Halichoeres it buries itself in the sand to sleep.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Females and juveniles are white with bold black stripes and eyespots on the fins, while terminal males turn green with orange lines and a dark spot at the tail base. A useful hunter of flatworms and small pest snails; also called Hoeven's wrasse.

region: Pacific — western Pacific to the Hawaiian Islands
description: Green with rows of red-pink scale markings and bold red bands on the head, a colour scheme that earned it the trade name "Christmas wrasse". It buries in sand at night and hunts small crustaceans by day.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa, Madagascar & the Mascarenes
description: A western Indian Ocean wrasse whose adults combine an orange-brown body with a paler, pink-lined head and a white-ringed black eyespot on the dorsal fin. It sleeps buried in the sand.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa & the Mascarenes to the Maldives
description: A small, peaceful sand-sleeper of the western Indian Ocean, green with pink stripes along the body and black eyespots on the dorsal fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Adults have a dark checkerboard of scale markings and a bright yellow spot below the dorsal fin; juveniles are black and white with the same yellow spot. A bold forager that turns over rubble for crustaceans and molluscs.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Green with bold red-pink lines and two white-ringed black eyespots on the dorsal fin — the "biocellatus" of its name. A peaceful, reef-safe sand-sleeper.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil
description: Terminal males have a yellow head, a black bar behind the pectoral fin and a blue-green rear; juveniles are bright yellow with a blue stripe. A common forager over Caribbean reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Caribbean to Brazil
description: A deeper-water Caribbean wrasse, yellow below with a broad navy-blue band along the back from head to tail. Large and robust, it hunts crabs and other invertebrates.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Terminal males are greenish with a large dark blotch on the mid-flank and red-lined heads, while initial-phase fish are white with a black midlateral stripe and yellow back.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: The largest Halichoeres, reaching half a metre in the wild; adults are blue-green with gold mottling and a dark spot at the base of the pectoral fin. It feeds on snails, crabs and urchins, and is mostly seen in public aquaria.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico
description: Common on shallow reefs, rubble and seagrass, and recognisable by two dark stripes along a pale greenish body. It dives into the sand when threatened and to sleep.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to New Caledonia
description: A wrasse of shallow lagoons and seagrass beds; adults are pale pastel green with faint darker markings, while juveniles are mottled green and brown for camouflage among the grass.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to Japan
description: Adults are dark blue-grey in front, shading abruptly to yellow over the rear half; juveniles are white with black stripes. It forages among coral and rubble on reef slopes.
